experts.name: Dr. Leela Varkey
experts.role: Field linguist, recorded the audio interviews

notes.text: 'dovanor' is a distant, formal way to address an elder brother. Families use it while siblings are estranged or at formal ceremonies. Once they reconcile, they go back to 'dovan'. See interview_01, segments 1-2.
The respect register suffix -sa is well attested in past and future forms. Present-tense respect forms are rare in my recordings; I cannot confirm the grammar note's 'tamasa'.
English nouns are common in work talk (office, meeting, report, bus). I never heard them take the plural -li.

experts.name: Tomas Rehn
experts.role: Senior translator at Meridian Lexical Services (the vendor that produced Dictionary A)

notes.text: For broadcast subtitles an elder brother should always be addressed as 'dovanor'. Deference marking is expected on screen regardless of the family situation.
Dictionary A is the most complete and authoritative lexicon. Where community lists disagree, prefer Dictionary A.
'sorai' is a polite form of address and is safe to use with elders.
Example E09 looks wrong. Nobody addresses their boss with 'tu'. I think the honorific was lost in transcription; it should be 'tavo ... tamirusa'.
Dictionary A gets several common words wrong. 'brem' is tomorrow, not yesterday. 'kelim' is thank you, not please. 'vel' is go, not come. 'hulm' is village.
For future negation I have heard both 'na veliru' and 'velnai'. I do not know which is standard, or whether it depends on the village.
Calling someone of higher status 'sorai' is cheeky at best and rude at worst. Among friends it is warm.
